newsitem.title: USA: Democrats, Republicans spar over disaster aid bill.
newsitem.headline: Democrats, Republicans spar over disaster aid bill.

text.p: Democratic lawmakers charged Wednesday that Republicans were forcing a delay in disaster relief for 23 states by using an emergency money bill to gain political leverage in budget talks.

Republican leaders responded that President Clinton need only lift his veto threat to set the $5.5 billion flowing to flood victims in the upper midwest and victims of other natural disasters around the country.

The Republican-dominated Senate Appropriations Committee, voting closely along party lines 15-13, approved the emergency funds with the controversial budget measure sponsored by their party. It would prevent any shutdown of government agencies this fall if Congress and the White House fail to agree on full year funds.

Senate Minority Leader Tom Daschle warned Republicans if they forced Clinton to carry out his veto threat, the battle would jeopardise chances of reaching a larger agreement to balance the budget and cut taxes.
"If the president has to veto this disaster bill I don't see any need to continue on the budget negotiations for the foreseeable future," the South Dakota Democrat said.
But Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott said they intended to move the disaster aid bill quickly. "We're not holding up anything," he said.

"We're going to send a disaster relief bill to the president. Now, if he wants to throw a temper tantrum over doing something that's right for the government and the American people, that's his problem," the Mississippi Republican said.
It also provides nearly $2 billion to pay for U.S. military operations in Bosnia and the no-fly zone in the Gulf.

Other problems cropped up for the emergency spending bill. House Democrats held a news conference to accuse Republicans of heartlessness for refusing to provide the full $76 million requested for the WIC (Women, Infants and Children) programme.

They compared the move to the Republicans' failed 1995 effort to reduce funding for the school lunch programme. But Republicans say there is more than enough money in the bill to keep all 7.4 million WIC recipients on the rolls.

Democrats plan to try to strip the automatic spending bill from the disaster relief legislation when it arrives before the full Senate. If they fail, Daschle predicted Clinton would veto it and Republicans would not muster the two-thirds vote necessary to override the veto. "It will not be overriden. We will see to that," he said.

The controversial provision was designed to prevent a replay of the budget battles that resulted in two government shutdowns when Congress and the White House disagreed over spending for the 1996 fiscal year.
The bill would continue government spending at 98 percent of the current year's level if funds are not approved and signed into law by the Oct. 1 start of the fiscal year.

Daschle and other Democratic senators said the lower funding would cause automatic cuts of seven percent across the board in all except mandatory benefit programmes. The total would be $35 billion below Clinton's request for fiscal 1998 funding.

Among the changes the automatic spending cut would force were -- elimination of 1,350 medical research projects, 700,000 mothers and children would lose nutrition funds each month, college aid would fall $1.8 billion, federal crop insurance would be eliminated and government computers would not be adjusted for the year 2000.
